To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the disuse of rat muscle induced by hindlimb suspension reduces the activity of protein kinase C, controlling the sarcolemmal chloride conductance, and increases muscle excitability, as measured by the rheobase.
disuse of rat soleus muscle in vivo reduces PKC activity controlling the sarcolema Cl conductance, which is responsible for muscle excitability.

the resting ClC-1 chloride conductance of sarcolemma (gCl) is reduced in control slow-twitch muscle compared to fast-twitch muscle and that the early increase of resting gCl in slow-twitch muscle after muscle disuse in vivo is entirely attributable to reduced PKC activity, most probably in the sarcolemma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of muscle excitability in the rat soleus muscle during muscle disuse induced by hindlimb suspension (HLS) in vivo.
the study of the mechanisms underlying disuse‐induc muscle atrophy, with particular reference to the role of protein kinases in the control of muscle excitability.
the study of muscle disuse induced by hindlimb suspension (HU), which causes atrophy and slow–fast fibre type transition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PKC activity is reduced in the soleus muscle of rats after 3 and 14 days of hindlimb unweighting, and this contributes to the early increase of the resting chloride conductance of sarcolemma.
the disuse‐inducing unloading reduces PKC activity and increases Cl‐channel activity, which is a mechanism of muscle atrophy and slow to fast transition.
the reduction of PKCα activity is the main mechanism responsible for ClC‐1 channel hyperpolarizing shift in Sol muscle fibre after 3 days HU, which in turn is responsible for the increased rheobase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the disuse of rat muscle induces a rapid and reversible reduction of PKC basal activity that controls the sarcolemma gCl, contributing to the early increase of muscle excitability.
the disuse of rat muscles induces the downregulation of PKC activity in the sarcolemma, with consequent increase in ClC‐1 Cl conductance and decrease in muscle excitability.
disuse of rat muscle reduces protein kinase C, which controls the sarcolemma ClC‐1 conductance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
disuse induces a rapid and significant decrease in PKC activity in muscle fibres, which contributes to muscle atrophy and impairment.

the early changes in the ClC‐1 channel conductance in Sol muscle during disuse are attributable to the modulation of PKC activity controlling ClC‐1 gating, which precedes and contributes to the slow‐to‐ fast transition.
disuse of skeletal muscle in vivo induces a rapid reduction of sarcolemma PKC activity, with consequences on muscle excitability and on ClC‐1 channel activity.
